## How-Tos

These how-tos assume you've worked through [Get Started](start-here.qmd) — you'll be
comfortable loading jstats, using `juse()` and `jload()`, and running the basic
functions. Each one stands on its own, so read whichever you need.

The How-Tos go beyond the Get Started on-ramp and point toward the fuller treatment
in the books. The menu on the left lists them by topic. The first article is
ready: [One-way ANOVA](anova.qmd), under Comparing groups. More are on the way,
and [Coming soon](coming-soon.qmd) describes them.

## Using the How-To pages {#using-the-how-to-pages}

Every How-To is built the same way, so what follows is said once, here, and not
repeated on each page.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Before you start"}
To follow along with any How-To you'll need:

- **R, RStudio, and jstats installed.** If they're not, work through
  [Get Started, Steps 1-5](start-here.qmd) first and come back.
- **An RStudio Project open**, so your working directory and files are already
  set up.
- **A new, empty R script open** (File > New File > R Script). You'll copy each
  numbered block into it, one at a time, running each before moving on.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How to use the How-To pages"}
The numbered blocks on a How-To page build one script. Paste each block into the
same R script file as you reach it, in order. By the end, the whole file runs
from top to bottom, except where a comment says an error is deliberate (so you
can see what one looks like).

- Every block starts with a dashed comment header (`## ---- 1. ... ----`). The
  header marks where one block ends and the next begins in your growing script,
  and RStudio reads those headers as sections, so they appear in the script's
  outline for easy jumping around.
- Block 1 of every page loads jstats and chooses the practice dataset that page
  uses, so each page's script runs on its own, in a fresh session.
- Run lines the way the [RStudio Orientation](rstudio-orientation.qmd) showed:
  cursor on the line, then Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) or the Run button;
  highlight several lines to run them together. Experiment freely as you go.
- Under most blocks, a Console pane shows what you should see when you run the
  block: the blue command lines, the gray notices, the tables with their red
  titles, and a red error where one is meant to happen. The panes show the code
  being run, along with any note written on the end of a command line, but not
  the standalone `##` comment lines (running one just echoes it back and does
  nothing).
- The boxes under an output are optional reading, and each title says who the
  box is for. **If you're new to statistics** explains what the analysis is
  for. **Reading this output** walks through what was printed. **Why jstats
  does it this way** explains the design, and how base R differs. **Coming from
  SPSS, Stata, or SAS?** gives the parallels in commercial statistical software.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The finished script on each page"}
Each How-To ends with a download: the *finished* version of the script you built
on that page. Finished means something specific. A goal every experienced
programmer and statistician takes for granted, but new researchers are rarely
told: a completed script should run from beginning to end without errors. Where
a page shows an error on purpose, the download has that line commented out, with
a note saying why, so the file runs clean.

To prove a script is finished, use the **Source** icon (to the right of Run in
the script toolbar): it runs the whole file, top to bottom, in one go. Source
shows the *output* without echoing each command back to the Console — that is
normal — and the small arrow beside Source offers "Source with Echo" if you
would like the commands shown too.

We recommend working through a page's blocks one at a time first: you learn far
more by building the script yourself and watching each piece run than by reading
a finished file. If you're keeping the download — and it's worth keeping, since
finished scripts travel — give it a proper home. In the **Files** tab of the
lower-right pane, click **New Folder** and type a name into the popup. "Scripts"
is a good one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reset your session"}
Experimenting means the occasional wrong turn — a setting changed, a practice
dataset overwritten, output that suddenly looks different. When something feels
off and you'd like a clean footing without restarting RStudio, run these two
lines in the Console:

```r
## Put jstats' output settings back to their defaults
joutput("standard")   # output level, and decimal places back to 3

## Point saving and loading back at your working directory
joptions(data.dir = NULL)
```

That resets jstats itself. To clear away objects you created while following
along, the simplest way is the little **broom** icon at the top of the
**Environment** pane (upper-right): one click sweeps the pane clean. It clears
*everything* in the Environment, so use it when you're between run-throughs, not
in the middle of one. The built-in practice datasets come right back whenever
you want them, with `jload("community")` or `jload("clinic")`.
:::

**Missing values, on every page.** Every jstats function sets aside the missing
values in your data before it computes anything. That includes codes such as −99
that have been *declared* as missing, whether the declaration arrived with an
SPSS, Stata, or SAS file or you made it yourself with `jdeclare_missing()`. Base
R does not do this for a code declared the SPSS way, and neither do many add-on
packages: to them the −99 is an ordinary number, and it goes into the mean. The
declaring is your part.
*[Telling jstats about missing values](missing-values.qmd)* shows how to declare
codes, and how to find codes that nobody has declared.
